turns.text: Can you describe the moment you first learned you would be sent down from Shanghai to the countryside? What did your home feel like that day?

I remember the air in our apartment felt heavy, like a curtain had been drawn across the windows even though the light was still coming in. My mother was quiet, folding clothes in the corner, and my sisters watched me with wide eyes, not sure if they should be proud or afraid for me. The announcement came in a meeting at school, not at home, but the real impact landed when I walked through our front door and saw my father sitting at the table, staring at the wall instead of at me. No one said much. There was a sense that any word could make things worse, or maybe just more real. I felt both singled out and invisible, like I was already halfway gone. The apartment, usually noisy and crowded, seemed to shrink around me, every sound muffled except for the clock ticking over the stove. I kept thinking about the city outside—the smell of coal smoke, the shouts from the alley—and wondered if I’d ever see it the same way again.

The way you describe the silence and the tension in your home makes it feel like the news changed everything, even before you left. You mentioned your mother folding clothes quietly—did she ever say anything to you, or show how she felt about you going?

She didn’t say much at first, just kept folding and refolding the same shirt, her hands moving slower than usual. Later that night, when my sisters were asleep, she sat on the edge of my bed and placed her hand on my shoulder. She didn’t cry. Instead, she asked if I had enough warm clothes, if my shoes were sturdy enough, and told me to keep my papers safe. She pressed a steamed bun into my hand for the train, like I was a child again. I could feel how much she wanted to say, but she only said, “Don’t lose yourself.” Her voice was so quiet I almost missed it. I think she was afraid that if she let herself really talk, she wouldn’t be able to stop. 

What I remember most is how she avoided my eyes, as if looking at me would make my leaving real. She woke up before dawn the day I left to sew an extra pocket inside my coat, just in case I needed to hide money or a letter. That was her way of saying everything she couldn’t.

I still remember the feel of her fingers, rough from years of laundry, moving quickly with the needle through the lining of my coat. She worked in the half-dark, her breath shallow and careful. That pocket became something I touched every day out there, even when it was empty. It was like carrying a piece of her worry stitched into my clothes. I never used it for money—there was never any extra—but I did keep a photograph tucked inside for a while, until the corners curled from damp and sweat. Sometimes, when I was standing in the fields with mud up to my knees, I’d press my hand against that spot and feel a little less alone.

Her silence stayed with me longer than any advice could have. It made me question what I was supposed to hold onto, and what I was supposed to let go. I think she wanted me to come back the same person, but she knew that was impossible.

The image of you standing in the fields, pressing your hand to that secret pocket, says so much about how you carried your family with you. You mentioned keeping a photograph there—what was in the photo, and what did it mean to you when you looked at it out in Beidahuang?

The photo was of my family crowded together in front of a faded wall, my sisters squinting into the sun, my father with his hand resting awkwardly on my mother’s shoulder. My mother’s hair was pinned up neatly, and I could see the outline of our apartment window behind us. I remember the day it was taken—someone had borrowed a camera, and we all tried to look serious, but my youngest sister kept giggling. 

Out in the fields, when I looked at that photo, it was like a window I could crawl through for a minute—back to the smell of rice cooking, the scratchy blanket on my bed, the sound of my sisters fighting over a book. Sometimes, after a long day when my arms ached and my face was stung by wind, I’d take it out just to remind myself that I hadn’t always been just another body in a line of strangers. The faces in that photo reminded me I was still someone’s child, someone’s sibling, even if I felt like I was disappearing into the mud. I think I was afraid that if I forgot those details, I’d lose the thread that tied me to who I was before.

Some nights, after the lamps went out and the others had fallen asleep, I’d take the photo out and trace their faces with my finger. The paper grew soft and thin, the edges stained from my hands. The photo wasn’t just a memory; it was proof that another life had existed, one where I could laugh and be clumsy, where I wasn’t always being watched or measured. In Beidahuang, everything was about blending in, surviving, not drawing attention. That little rectangle of home was defiant—it insisted that I had roots, that I wasn’t just a mouth to feed or a pair of hands for labor. When the loneliness pressed in, I’d hold the photo against my chest and try to remember the sound of my sisters’ laughter in the stairwell, the way my mother’s voice softened when she called us for dinner. It was both comfort and a kind of ache, because the more I needed it, the further away that world seemed.

Tracing the faces in the dark, feeling the paper thin out, sounds like a ritual that kept your old life alive even as it faded. You mentioned how everything in Beidahuang was about blending in and not drawing attention—was there ever a moment when you slipped, when your city background showed through and set you apart from the others?

There were plenty of moments, especially early on, when I couldn’t hide where I came from. The first time I tried to carry water from the well, I spilled half of it before I even made it back to the yard. My hands were soft, not used to rope or splinters, and the villagers noticed right away. I remember one afternoon, I was asked to help slaughter a chicken. I’d never done it before—at home, meat came wrapped in paper from the market. I hesitated, and the knife shook in my hand. The others laughed, not cruelly, but with a kind of tired amusement. Someone took the knife from me and finished the job in two quick motions.

But it was my speech that gave me away the most. My accent was Shanghai, round and slippery compared to the clipped, nasal tones of the Northeast. I tried to copy their words, but I always tripped up. Once, I used a city slang word by accident, and everyone stopped what they were doing and stared at me. For a long moment, it was like I was a radio tuned to the wrong frequency. After that, I learned to keep my sentences short, my head down. It was lonely, biting back the urge to say things the way I’d always said them, but I knew the less I stood out, the safer I’d be.

The first winter, I made the mistake of wearing my city shoes out to the fields. They were thin and polished, more for walking on pavement than trudging through frozen earth. By midday, my toes were numb, and the mud had swallowed the soles. Someone handed me a pair of patched felt boots, rough and too big, and told me to get used to it. I felt exposed, like I was playing dress-up in someone else’s life. Even the way I ate was wrong—too slow, too careful. I watched the others tear into their food, hunched over tin bowls, and tried to copy them, but the hunger was different for me; it was new, not yet part of my bones.

There was a day when I tried to talk about a book I’d read back in Shanghai. The words dried up in my mouth when I saw the blank faces around me. Books were dangerous, and memories of school didn’t mean much when the work was breaking you down. That was when I realized how little my old life mattered here—how quickly it could become a liability. I learned to let my city habits slip away one by one, but some things clung to me, like the way I folded my clothes or the way I looked people in the eye. Those were harder to hide, and sometimes they made me a target, but I never quite managed to erase them.

Wearing your city shoes into the fields and talking about books must have made you feel out of place in a way that was hard to fix. You said hunger was new for you then—can you describe a time when you really felt that hunger, and how it changed the way you saw food or even yourself?

There was one day, late in the season, when the fields were nothing but frozen stalks and the wind cut through every layer of clothing. Lunch was a thin millet porridge, barely more than cloudy water, and a heel of bread so hard I had to soak it to chew. My stomach cramped, but I ate slowly, trying to make each bite last. By evening, the ache had spread through my whole body, dull and endless, like a bell ringing inside my bones. I remember looking at the others, how they scraped every last grain from their bowls, and I realized I was doing the same—licking my fingers, searching for crumbs on the table. 

Before Beidahuang, I never thought much about food. At home, there was always enough, even if it was simple. Now, I dreamed about rice, about the taste of oil, about the smell of dumplings steaming in a neighbor’s kitchen. I started to understand why people hid bits of food, why they counted every bean. Hunger made me smaller, meaner in some ways; I caught myself envying others, even feeling angry when someone got an extra ladle by luck or strength. It stripped away a layer of politeness I didn’t know I wore. I realized how quickly comfort could become just a memory, and how much of a person is shaped by what they lack.

Hunger made me notice things I’d never noticed before—the way someone’s hands shook when they lifted a bowl, the sound of teeth scraping against a spoon. I learned to eat without looking up, to guard my food with my body, to swallow quickly if someone glanced my way. There was a kind of shame in it, but also a stubbornness. I started saving scraps in my coat pocket, even when I knew they’d go stale or moldy. Sometimes, at night, I’d chew on a piece of dried root just to quiet the emptiness. I stopped thinking of food as pleasure; it became a kind of currency, a measure of luck or favor. The hunger never really left, even when the season changed. It settled deep, not just in my stomach but in my thinking—like a voice always reminding me how little it took to lose everything I’d once taken for granted.

The way you describe guarding your food and chewing on dried roots at night shows how hunger changed not just your body, but your sense of trust and comfort. You said the hunger never really left, even when the season changed—how did that lingering feeling affect you after you left Beidahuang, when you were back in the city or with family again?
